eraContext: Postwar convenience baking arrived with Betty Crocker and Duncan Hines boxed mixes, and the yellow layer cake with chocolate frosting became the default centerpiece of American birthdays and potlucks.
funFact: Early boxed cake mixes included powdered egg, but sales lagged — market research found bakers felt guilty using something so effortless. Manufacturers removed the powdered egg and required a fresh one instead, and sales took off once the process felt a little more like real baking.
modernInterpretation: It's still the default shape at most American bakeries and grocery store cake counters today — the two-layer round with chocolate frosting is the closest thing this app has to a baseline 'birthday cake.'

eraContext: The Tunnel of Fudge cake took second place in the 1966 Pillsbury Bake-Off, but home bakers loved it so much that Bundt pan sales exploded, cementing the bundt shape in American kitchens.
funFact: The original recipe relied on a specific frosting mix that was later discontinued, which briefly made the cake nearly impossible to replicate — Pillsbury eventually reworked the recipe around plain cocoa powder so it could survive the discontinuation.
modernInterpretation: The idea of engineering a cake around a deliberately gooey, underbaked center is a direct ancestor of the molten lava cakes and gooey-centered desserts that would define fine dining decades later.

eraContext: Published anonymously by a home cook in a 1978 issue of Southern Living, the Hummingbird Cake recipe spread by word of mouth across the American South and became the magazine's most-requested recipe ever.
funFact: No one has ever definitively confirmed where the name comes from — the most common theory is simply that the cake is sweet enough to attract hummingbirds, though the recipe itself has no connection to the bird.
modernInterpretation: It remains a fixture of Southern weddings and celebrations, and its banana-pineapple-pecan combination shows up regularly in the 'tropical spice' cakes bakeries build today.

eraContext: Riding the era's health-food-chic wave — carrots read as 'wholesome' even under a pound of cream cheese frosting — carrot cake graduated from health-food-store novelty to upscale bakery staple.
funFact: Carrot cake is actually much older than its 1980s heyday — carrots were used as a sugar substitute in cakes as far back as medieval Europe, and again during WWII-era rationing, long before it became a health-food symbol.
modernInterpretation: The cream cheese frosting it popularized became the default pairing for spiced cakes generally — it's now just as at home on red velvet or pumpkin cake as it is on carrot.

eraContext: Chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten popularized the molten center in the early 1990s after pulling an underbaked chocolate cake early by accident, and it became the defining status dessert of fine dining menus through the decade.
funFact: French pastry chefs had been deliberately underbaking chocolate desserts for years under other names before Vongerichten's version — his accident just happened to hit at the right cultural moment to make the technique famous in the US.
modernInterpretation: It's a defining early example of the 'engineered dessert' — bakers today purpose-build soft or molten centers into all kinds of cakes and cookies using the same underlying idea.

eraContext: Magnolia Bakery's cameo in Sex and the City kicked off a citywide cupcake-boutique boom, and red velvet's dramatic color made it the flagship flavor of the single-serving cake era.
funFact: Red velvet's original red tint came from a real chemical reaction between natural cocoa and buttermilk or vinegar, not food coloring — modern Dutch-processed cocoa reacts much less, which is why almost every recipe today adds red food coloring to compensate.
modernInterpretation: The cupcake-as-standalone-dessert format this era normalized paved the way for the individually-portioned cakes everywhere today, from mini layer cakes to cake pops.

eraContext: As baking went visual-first on Instagram, tall naked-style layer cakes finished with a glossy ganache drip became the decade's most photographed dessert, engineered for the feed as much as the fork.
funFact: The drip technique started as a professional trick for disguising an imperfect frosting job underneath — it wasn't originally meant to be the star of the cake, just camouflage.
modernInterpretation: The drip cake's visual-first logic evolved into today's textured-buttercream and modern-geometric wedding cake trends — still built for the camera, just less literal about it.

eraContext: A deliberately scorched, crustless cheesecake from a San Sebastián bar went viral on TikTok and Instagram, turning imperfection into the decade's defining aesthetic after ten years of flawless drip cakes.
funFact: The recipe traces back to La Viña, a bar in San Sebastián, Spain, whose owner has said the burnt top wasn't originally a stylistic choice at all — it's just how the cheesecake came out of a very hot oven.
modernInterpretation: It kicked off a broader 'anti-perfection' movement in home baking that now shows up as deliberately rustic, imperfect finishes across many cake styles, not just cheesecake.
